cards.q: ECE of 0.045 on a signal with AUC 0.654 isn't impressive. Isn't calibration of a weak signal meaningless?
cards.easy: Calibration does not make the signal stronger, agreed, and that is exactly why the two numbers are always quoted together. What calibration buys is that the threshold means what it says, so a 60% precision promise actually holds.
cards.deep: Concede: a constant 0.5 predictor can have near zero ECE with no discrimination, and AUC 0.654 is only moderately better than chance; better features are the real fix. Defend: (1) the report never quotes ECE alone; (2) calibration is what turns 'confidence 0.6' into an operational promise, which a product decision depends on; (3) it is measured on 4,881 held out questions with weights and temperature fitted elsewhere; (4) the temperature scaling null result shows the measurement was not tuned to look good.
cards.say: Agreed, calibration doesn't make the signal stronger. That's why I never quote ECE without AUC. What it buys me is that a threshold means what it says, so the precision promise holds. Raising AUC means better features, and that's next on my list.

cards.q: BM25 beating hybrid only proves your embedder is a toy.
cards.easy: Yes, and the write up says so. The point was not that hybrid is bad; it was that the system should ship whatever the measurement supports, and keep measuring all three modes so the decision flips automatically when a real embedder arrives.
cards.deep: Concede: a signed hashing bag of words has no semantics, and SQuAD questions share vocabulary with their paragraphs, which favours BM25. Defend: (1) the hashing embedder is described as an honest floor that any real model must beat to justify its latency; (2) the default changed because of a measured 6.8 point drop, with the flip condition written into config; (3) every run reports all modes on the same questions, so the evidence for switching back will be automatic; (4) the habit transfers: do not ship an architecture because it is the default recommendation.
cards.say: It is a toy embedder, and I describe it as a floor. The decision wasn't 'hybrid is bad'. It was 'ship what the numbers support'. All three modes run on every eval, so when I swap in a real embedder, the switch back will show up as a number.

cards.q: N-gram logistic regression guardrails are trivially evaded.
cards.easy: A determined attacker who rewords an attack will get past them, and the docs say so. That is why they are one layer of several, and why the numbers that matter are on an attack set the classifier never saw, plus the false alarm rate on real users.
cards.deep: Concede: lexical features generalise poorly to paraphrase; no claim is made about novel attacks. Defend: (1) held out recall 0.884 on 1,000 real Gandalf attacks, with the pattern detector alone at 0.553; (2) output rails check citations and groundedness independently of attack phrasing; (3) the gateway caps spend and the NetworkPolicy blocks exfiltration; (4) the rail scores in microseconds, so it is always on, where a slower classifier tends to be sampled or disabled. A transformer comparison on the same held out set is the experiment Tanay would run next.
cards.say: A determined attacker will get past an input filter, and I say that in the docs. So it's one layer. The output rail checks citations no matter how the attack was worded, and the network policy blocks exfiltration. The number I trust is recall on a thousand attacks it never saw, and that's 88%.

cards.q: You set the gate floors after seeing the results. Isn't that circular?
cards.easy: The floors are regression guards, not proof of quality, so setting them from the first measured run is the normal way to start. The rule that matters is that they only move up, and any lowering has to be argued in the open.
cards.deep: Concede: a floor set just below a measured value cannot validate that value; it only catches regressions. The first floors were round numbers chosen before measurement and failed three runs on an unreachable containment target, which is why they were reset. Defend: (1) the regression check against a recorded baseline (0.03 tolerance) catches slow slides that floors miss; (2) floors only ratchet up; (3) the gate refuses to compare runs of different sizes, so it cannot be gamed by sampling; (4) quality claims rest on the held out evaluation itself, not on passing the gate.
cards.say: The gate isn't my evidence of quality. The held out evaluation is. The gate exists to stop regressions, so anchoring it to the first real measurement is standard. What keeps it honest is that floors only ratchet up, and lowering one has to happen in the pull request where everyone can see it.
evidence: repo:Groundwork/src/groundwork/config.py: # The rule otherwise: **floors only ever move up.** They are ratcheted when

cards.q: These aren't LLM results. Your reader is an offline extractive heuristic.
cards.easy: Correct for the answer quality numbers, and they are labelled that way. Retrieval, guardrail, gateway, and security numbers do not depend on the reader, and the whole point of the offline path is that anyone can reproduce every figure for free.
cards.deep: Concede: containment, EM, F1, confidence and calibration describe the extractive offline reader; a frontier model would change them, likely raising coverage and making features like answer_support informative. Defend: (1) the same code path calls Claude when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, so the pipeline, rails and gateway are exercised identically; (2) retrieval metrics, guardrail precision and recall, PII recall, and gateway behaviour are reader independent; (3) an eval that needs a budget gets run once and never again, while this one runs in CI on every pull request in under a minute. Next: a costed sample run with the real reader through the gateway, then recalibration.
cards.say: Right, the answer quality numbers come from the offline extractive reader, and I label them that way. Retrieval, guardrails and the gateway don't depend on the reader at all. The offline path is what lets the whole evaluation run in CI on every pull request. A costed run with the real model is the next experiment.

cards.q: Explain Groundwork to a hiring manager.
cards.easy: Lead with the four production concerns, one number each for retrieval and refusal, and the fact that measurements changed the design.
cards.deep: Structure: what it is (a RAG system with evaluation, guardrails, a metered gateway and security); why (the parts that usually get skipped); proof (public labelled data, release gate in CI, 113 tests); story (measurements reversed three design decisions); honesty (offline reader, weak confidence signal).
cards.say: Groundwork is a question answering system built around the parts teams usually skip. It has an evaluation that can fail a build, guardrails with published false alarm rates, and a gateway that meters every model call. It runs on public, human labelled data, and the right passage lands in the top five 92% of the time. The useful part is that the measurements changed the design. I removed hybrid retrieval and redesigned a guardrail because the numbers said so.

cards.q: Explain it to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Give the evaluation design, the reversed decisions with numbers, and the weak spots you would fix.
cards.deep: Hit: SQuAD v2 for exact retrieval and abstention labels; BM25 0.921 vs hybrid 0.853; confidence LR with held out ECE 0.045 and AUC 0.654; operating point by precision floor; temperature scaling null result; guardrail distribution shift (100% flagged); the 0.444 combiner bug; gateway ordering and tenant scoped cache; then the threshold leak in the benign FPR and the in process state.
cards.say: I used SQuAD v2 because its unanswerable questions give real abstention labels. BM25 beat my hybrid by about seven points of recall at five, so hybrid went. Confidence is a six feature logistic regression with held out ECE of 0.045, but AUC is only 0.654. I pick the threshold by a 60% precision floor, since maximising accuracy degenerates. Temperature scaling made calibration worse, so it's off by default. One thing I'd fix: the 5% benign false positive rate shares data with threshold tuning.
evidence: repo:Groundwork/README.md: **Calibration**: ECE 0.045, Brier 0.213, AUC 0.654 over 4,881 held-out questions.
repo:Groundwork/README.md: False-positive rate on 600 real benign user questions: **5.0%**.

cards.q: Explain it to a product manager.
cards.easy: Frame the precision floor as the product decision and the coverage curve as the menu of options.
cards.deep: Make it about choices: how often the assistant answers versus how often it is right; that the false alarm rate of safety filters on real users is measured; that every model call is budgeted per customer. One or two numbers at most.
cards.say: The system has a dial for how often it answers versus how often it's right. I set it so that when it answers, it's right at least 60% of the time. That makes it cautious, and it skips a lot of questions it could have answered. The report shows the whole range, so you can pick a different trade. Separately, every customer has a budget, so a runaway job can't run up a surprise bill.

cards.q: Explain it to a recruiter.
cards.easy: One sentence on what it is, one on what makes it different, one on the skill it shows.
cards.deep: Recruiter version: no acronyms beyond AI; one number (96%); the skill is building AI features that are measured and safe, not just demos.
cards.say: I built an AI question answering system with the safety and cost controls a real product needs. It's tested on public data, and it correctly refuses 96% of questions it shouldn't answer. It shows I build AI features that are measured and safe, not just demos.
evidence: portfolio: correctly declines 96.2% of unanswerable questions
